title: Loss metric cannot compare across different critic architectures
description: The authors caution that the constant scaling factor depending on the critic's architecture means it is hard to compare models with different critics using the WGAN loss metric.

verdict.reasoning: The single assessed paper ("Wasserstein GANs Work Because They Fail") explicitly acknowledges the scaling-factor problem (Remark 3.1) and even notes that normalizing by the Lipschitz constant "should be considered," but it does not propose, implement, or evaluate any concrete method for enabling fair cross-architecture comparison of WGAN loss metrics. Its focus is on demonstrating that WGAN loss does not approximate the Wasserstein distance, not on solving the comparability gap. No other papers address the gap. Therefore the gap remains open.

paper.title: Wasserstein GANs Work Because They Fail (to Approximate the Wasserstein Distance)
paper.abstract: Wasserstein GANs are based on the idea of minimising the Wasserstein distance between a real and a generated distribution. We provide an in-depth mathematical analysis of differences between the theoretical setup and the reality of training Wasserstein GANs. In this work, we gather both theoretical and empirical evidence that the WGAN loss is not a meaningful approximation of the Wasserstein distance. Moreover, we argue that the Wasserstein distance is not even a desirable loss function for deep generative models, and conclude that the success of Wasserstein GANs can in truth be attributed to a failure to approximate the Wasserstein distance.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper provides an in-depth analysis showing that WGAN loss does not meaningfully approximate the Wasserstein distance, and argues that this failure is actually beneficial for generative performance. It discusses the scaling factor issue (where optimizing over K-Lipschitz functions scales the estimate by K) and notes that normalization by the Lipschitz constant should be considered, but this is in service of showing WGAN-GP fails to approximate Wasserstein distance, not as a solution for cross-architecture comparison.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not address the gap of comparing loss metrics across different critic architectures. While it acknowledges the scaling factor issue (Remark 3.1) and suggests normalizing by the Lipschitz constant, it does not propose or evaluate any method for enabling fair comparison of WGAN loss values across models with different critic architectures. The paper's focus is on showing that WGAN loss is not a meaningful Wasserstein distance approximation, not on solving the cross-architecture comparability problem.
evidence_snippets: As pointed out in [CITE:WGAN] if we optimise over the set of $K$-Lipschitz functions instead of the set of $1$-Lipschitz functions, then the estimate of Wasserstein distance scales by the same factor, i.e. $\max_{\substack{\normLpz{f}\leq K}}\left( \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p^\ast}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p^\theta}[f(x)]\right) = K W_1(p^\ast,p^\theta)$.
Since the 1-Lipschitz continuity of $D_\alpha$ is  only approximately enforced in WGAN-GP, a normalisation by the Lipschitz constant of $D_\alpha$ should be considered.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: Moderately tractable. The problem is well-scoped (fixing a known scaling ambiguity) and admits plausible approaches: normalizing by the Lipschitz constant (as the paper itself suggests), using spectral normalization to enforce a fixed Lipschitz constant across architectures, or empirically estimating the scaling factor via reference generators. Compute requirements are modest (training standard WGANs). Evaluability is clear — successful normalization would yield consistent loss rankings across architectures on held-out quality metrics (e.g., FID/Inception). The main caveat lowering the score is that the WGAN loss does not reliably approximate the Wasserstein distance even for a single critic, so a "fixed" scaling factor may not make cross-architecture comparisons truly meaningful — deeper methodological work may be needed to establish what the normalized loss actually measures.
